Catatonia or Depression - A Diagnostic Dilemma in Stiff Person 
Syndrome: A rare case report 
Dr Dhritiman Das, Dr Harkishan Mamtani, Dr Krishna Prasad 
Junior Resident, MD-2, Department of Psychiatry, NIMHANS, PDF in 
Neuropsychiatry, NIMHANS, Additional Professor, Department of 
Psychiatry, NIMHANS 
Introduction: Stiff person syndrome(SPS) is an autoimmune 
neurological disorder that presents with severe progressive stiffness 
of axial muscles and severe spasms. Its incidence and prevalence are 
around 1-2 per million population. This condition is diagnosed using 
criteria, clinical presentation, and classical EMG findings and antibody 
testing. Anti- GAD antibody inhibits Glutamic Acid Decarboxylase 
which synthesizes GABA from glutamate. Deficiency of GABA in CNS is 
supposed to result in SPS. Anxiety and depression are two most 
common psychiatric symptoms reported in SPS. Catatonia and 
Conversion Disorder are two most common differential diagnoses 
with SPS due to similar clinical presentation. Benzodiazepines are the 
first line drug used for symptomatic therapy. Intravenous 
Immunoglobulin(IVIG) , corticosteroids and Plasma Exchange(PLEX) 
are modes of immunotherapy to such patients. SSRIs are the first line 
of treatment for anxiety and depression in such patients. 
Case Description: 70 year old woman presents with gradually 
progressive stiffness and spasms involving both extremities and trunk 
with difficulty in walking since past 2 years. She was provisionally 
diagnosed with SPS after classical EMG findings (with IV Diazepam 
test) and ruled out all other differential diagnoses after thorough 
investigations and clinical examination. Anti-GAD antibody was 
negative in this case. Paraneoplastic cause was suspected. 
Neuropsychiatry referral was sought in view of persistent crying 
spells and disturbed sleep.

Discussion: Patient was difficult to be interviewed due to dysarthric 
speech and continuous crying spells. At initial presentation, catatonia 
was suspected due to presenting features as per BFCRS scale. But this 
diagnosis was ruled out after the Lorazepam Challenge test. After 
thorough history taking and MSE, anankastic traits were discovered 
prior to onset of illness and a provisional diagnosis of moderate 
depression was kept in view of depressed cognitions and passive 
death wishes secondary to difficulty in accepting diagnosis and its 
related disability. Tab Mirtzapine was initiated upto 15 mg for 
depression and Tab Quetiapine was initiated at 25 mg HS for sleep 
disturbances and crying spells secondary to spasms in supine which 
she tolerated well. She was treated with IVIG,PLEX, IVMP, Diazepam, 
tizanidine and baclofen for stiffness in SPS. 
Conclusion: SPS is a rare neurological condition which can mimic 
presentations of catatonia and conversion disorder resulting in 
diagnostic dilemma. Neurological and psychiatric features interplay 
with each other in SPS. SPS, anxiety, depression and substance use 
disorders are all manifestations of underlying GABA dysfunction.
